name: Tyrian Purple
poem: Wrung from the gland of a sea snail, ten thousand of them for a single hem — a colour so costly it became the law of kings.

recipe.note: A dark red-violet — crimson married to deep blue, then dimmed.

lenses.label: Art History
lenses.intro: The most expensive dye in the ancient world — worth more by weight than gold, and reserved by law for those who could afford to wear it.

entries.title: Justinian and His Court
entries.meta: Mosaic · Basilica of San Vitale, Ravenna · c. 547
entries.blurb: The Emperor Justinian stands in Tyrian purple at the centre of the apse mosaic — a colour that doubles as a claim to divine right.

entries.title: The Codex Argenteus
entries.blurb: Silver and gold letters of a Wulfila-translated Bible written on vellum dyed Tyrian purple — text so precious the parchment had to match.

entries.title: Portrait of a Roman Woman
entries.blurb: The wife of a successful baker, painted in a purple-bordered stola — a stripe-width regulated by sumptuary law down to the finger.

lenses.label: Fashion
lenses.intro: Purple was less a colour than a credential — sumptuary laws across the ancient world spelled out who could wear which stripe.

entries.title: The Imperial Toga
entries.blurb: A solid Tyrian purple toga embroidered with gold — worn only by triumphant generals, then only by emperors. Anyone else caught wearing it could be executed.

entries.title: The Byzantine Loros
entries.blurb: A long jewelled scarf of purple silk, wrapped diagonally across the emperor's chest — the only article of clothing that needed no further explanation of rank.

entries.title: Cadbury Purple
entries.blurb: A specific shade of purple chosen in tribute to Queen Victoria, trademarked by Cadbury and ferociously defended in court for over a century.

lenses.label: Nature
lenses.intro: Every drop of Tyrian purple was wrenched from a living animal — the dye's history is also a history of slaughter.

entries.title: The Murex Snail
entries.blurb: The mucus from a single gland, exposed to air and sunlight, oxidises through yellow and green to deep purple. Ten thousand snails yielded one gram of dye.

entries.title: The Shell Mounds of Tyre
entries.blurb: Millennia of broken murex shells piled into hills along the coast — archaeological evidence of an industry that crashed an entire species.

entries.title: The Purple Sea Urchin
entries.blurb: Unrelated to dye but glowing with the same Tyrian hue — pigment from the urchin's diet of algae, kept in its spines as both signal and armour.

lenses.label: Pop Culture
lenses.intro: When the ancient dye finally died out, the colour itself kept its old meanings — power, scarcity, theatre.

entries.title: The Color Purple
entries.blurb: The novel's title points to a colour rarely seen by its narrator — wildflowers in a field, beauty God supposedly gets angry if we walk past unnoticed.

entries.title: Purple Rain
entries.blurb: Prince's signature colour and signature record — a hue chosen for its associations with royalty, mysticism, and the bruised edge of pop.

entries.title: The Purple Heart
entries.blurb: The oldest decoration still awarded — a small heart of purple enamel given to those wounded or killed in service, a colour chosen for its associations with sacrifice.

lenses.label: Etymology
lenses.intro: The colour's name is also a place — and an entire civilisation took its name from the colour.

entries.title: Tyre
entries.blurb: The ancient port that produced the finest grade — "Tyrian purple" was simply the city's main export, prized across the Mediterranean.

entries.title: "Phoenicia"
entries.blurb: The Greeks called the murex-dyeing people "phoinikēs" — literally "purple people." The civilisation took its identity from the colour it made.

entries.title: "Porphyra"
entries.blurb: The Greek word for the murex snail and its dye — and the source of every modern European word for the colour, including "purple" itself.

lenses.label: Symbolism
lenses.intro: Across cultures the colour signals power, but the kind of power keeps shifting — emperor, bishop, pop star.

entries.title: "Born in the Purple"
entries.blurb: An imperial child born in the purple-walled birthing chamber of the Boukoleon palace — a literal birth into the colour, securing the right to rule.

entries.title: The Bishop's Cassock
entries.blurb: Bishops wear purple cassocks during Lent — a colour of penitence in Christian liturgy, drawing on its older associations with sovereignty held in restraint.

entries.title: Mourning Purple
entries.blurb: While Western mourning wears black, Thai widows historically wore purple — a colour reserved for those grieving the king or a close royal.
